title: Cristaux et cohomologie de De Rham : généralités, correspondances Deligne et Berthelot (1965-1969) : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous pages compute the cohomology of O on the stratifying/de Rham site through cosimplicial rings of completed diagonals. To replace stratifications by crystals one needs divided-power (PD) neighbourhoods. This page therefore builds the PD envelope.

Problem. Given a ring A and an ideal I, find an A-algebra B with a PD ideal (J, γ) and a map u: A → B with u(I) ⊂ J, universal for these data. In modern terms B is the divided-power envelope D_A(I).

Construction. Take the polynomial algebra over A on symbols Γ^n(x), for x ∈ I and n ≥ 2, with Γ^1(x) := x. Divide by the relations:
- Γ^n(x+y) = Γ^n x + Γ^n y + Σ_{p+q=n, p,q≥1} Γ^p(x)Γ^q(y);
- Γ^n(ax) = a^n Γ^n(x), for a ∈ A;
- Γ^m(x)Γ^n(x) = binom(m+n, m) Γ^{m+n}(x).
The composition relation Γ^m(Γ^n x) = (mn)!/((n!)^m m!) Γ^{mn}(x) is written and then struck out. J is the ideal generated by the Γ^n(x) with n ≥ 1. Grothendieck notes that it remains to check universality, i.e. that J really carries divided powers. This is the Roby/Berthelot point: the composition axiom comes for free once one works in Γ_A(I).

Second part. Assume A is a Z_(p)-algebra (his Z_{pZ}). Write n = Σ a_i p^i in base p. Legendre's formula gives v_p(n!) = Σ a_i v_p((p^i)!), with v_p((p^i)!) = (p^i − 1)/(p − 1). Hence in any PD ideal one has γ^n(x) = c_n γ^1(x)^{a_0} γ^p(x)^{a_1} ⋯ γ^{p^ν}(x)^{a_ν}. Here c_n is the prime-to-p part of Π((p^i)!)^{a_i}/n!; on the next page it is shown to be a unit of Z_(p).

So the envelope is generated by the [x, ν] = Γ^{p^ν}(x). The next page looks for a minimal set of relations among these, e.g. Γ^{p^ν}(x)^p = (p^{ν+1})!/((p^ν)!)^p · Γ^{p^{ν+1}}(x). It then starts the case of a principal ideal I = (λ). This is the standard p-local reduction: a PD structure on a Z_(p)-algebra is determined by γ_p.
errors: Linearity relation written as Γ^n(xy) = x^n Γ^n(y) with x ∈ I, y ∈ A. The roles are swapped: it should read Γ^n(ax) = a^n Γ^n(x) with a ∈ A, x ∈ I, since Γ^n(y) is undefined for y ∉ I.
'v_p(n) = Σ a_i v_p(p^ν)' should read v_p(n!) = Σ a_i v_p((p^i)!), with v_p((p^i)!) = (p^i − 1)/(p − 1). Grothendieck writes n for n! and ν for i.
'J idéal engendré par les Γ^n(x) (n ≥ 1, x ∈ J)' is circular; it should be x ∈ I.

The PD property of J (in particular the composition axiom and well-definedness of γ on sums of generators) is left as 'à vérifier'. It is a genuine nontrivial step, settled by Roby's theory of Γ_A(M).

ideas.what: Universal A-algebra with PD ideal containing the image of I, by generators and relations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Berthelot (thesis 1974, Cohomologie cristalline); building on Roby (1963-65) and Cartan seminar (1954-55)
ideas.where_published: Sketched in 'Crystals and the de Rham cohomology of schemes' (Dix exposés, 1968), where PD neighbourhoods are used

ideas.what: Over Z_(p), γ_n is determined by γ_{p^i} via base-p digits of n, with a p-adic unit coefficient (Legendre's formula)
ideas.modern_name: Reduction of PD structures to γ_p over Z_(p)-algebras
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard (Berthelot; Berthelot–Ogus, Notes on crystalline cohomology)

ideas.what: Presentation of the PD envelope by generators [x, ν] = Γ^{p^ν}(x), and the principal-ideal case
ideas.modern_name: Explicit PD envelope of a principal ideal, e.g. Z_(p)⟨t⟩

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine working-out of the PD envelope and the standard p-local simplification, both well established in Berthelot's work and Roby's. It is historically interesting only as evidence that Grothendieck was constructing PD hulls himself around 1965-66, before Berthelot's thesis.
transcription_corrections: 'Z_{pZ}' means Z localized at the prime pZ, i.e. Z_(p).
'v_p(n) = Σ a_i v_p(p^ν)' is what is written, but the intended meaning is v_p(n!) = Σ a_i v_p((p^i)!).
In 'Γ^n(xy) = x^n Γ^n(y)' the intended reading is Γ^n(ax) = a^n Γ^n(x), a ∈ A.
The generator range in 'J idéal engendré par ...' is probably x ∈ I (the image is ambiguous).
